...Night is coming on, and we have to leave this place.
But before we go, look at the white breath in the air. That is the mark of us being alive. And look ahead of you, too: beneath the damp earth lie our classmates.
There is rust and gunsmoke in the air here. This is not a university lecture hall in Deity Grypherburg. Look around you—the empty place on the left belonged to 'Pencil Stub.' He always had paper and a pen on him, fussing over those flowery scripts of his, and yet he was the first to answer me, the first willing to clench his fist and stand up and fight back.
That open patch in the middle is where Nika and Yeremey used to sit. I think I can still see Nika smiling shyly, thumping Yeremey on the back, singing that off-key school song over and over until she drank herself under the table.
And Fadey—whatever he had done wrong before, he never once forgot where his duty lay. In that last moment, he left the chance to live to somebody else.
...
I could go on naming names like these for a long time. I want to keep going, honestly, until every last one of them is set down in our hearts.
But believe me: your grief and mine is not weakness, and still less is it cowardice. It is a notch cut into us, and it records the struggle and the rebirth of these ten days. It tells us that there are some things which can never be taken away.
We will remember that on a bitter winter's day, in a sea of fire that swallowed everything, we held on tight to one another's hands.
The dust in the air, the songs we never finished, the tears that fell into the snow, the battlefield that was ours... so long as even one person remembers—
they are alive, and so are we!
Ursus cannot kill us. No permafrost is thick enough to seal in every root; there is always some stubborn living thing down there, crawling and growing.
We must remember their faces, remember how they fought, and above all we must remember that in that future they died for—we will meet every one of them again in the end.
Come, then. One last time, follow me, and say all their names aloud. Say them for the fallen and say them for the standing; say them for our yesterday and say them for our tomorrow!

One night some time afterward, while clearing out odds and ends, Sonya turned up several ruined school uniforms. They had been wrapped up tight, without a speck of dust on them.
She ran a hand slowly over her burning cheek, her fingertips numb and trembling—the speech she had given that day before the graveyard in the Katorga District came pouring back into her, word by word, like snowflakes striking a windowpane.
'General Zima, what are you still doing in here? Everyone's waiting for you.'
'Stop rushing her, Leto. It's a party to celebrate a victory—of course Sonya's going to take her time getting ready.'
They would meet them again somewhere better... and even if it fell short of perfect, a great deal had still been done, hadn't it?
So Sonya paused, let the faintest of smiles show, and then offhandedly began complaining to everyone about Ursus winters as she rubbed her hands hard together.
